VOO vs. QQQ: Here's the ETF I'd Personally Buy and Hold for Decades
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool

Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO) and Invesco's QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ) are both popular exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for long-term investors. VOO tracks the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), while QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100.

Vanguard launched VOO in 2010 as the ETF version of the Vanguard S&P 500 Index Fund, which was launched in 1976. Invesco launched QQQ in 1999. Over the past 10 years, VOO has delivered a total return of 318% with reinvested dividends, while QQQ has generated an even bigger total return of 533%. Let's see why QQQ outperformed VOO by such a wide margin -- and if it's still the better ETF to buy today.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
The differences between VOO and QQQ

VOO and QQQ are both passively managed funds that automatically track their underlying indexes, so they charge much lower fees than actively managed funds. VOO charges an expense ratio of 0.03%, while QQQ charges an expense ratio of 0.18%.

VOO is more broadly diversified because the S&P 500 tracks the country's top 500 companies by market capitalization. The index is rebalanced every quarter to add faster-growing companies and drop weaker ones, so its investors are always exposed to market leaders.

QQQ holds fewer stocks because the Nasdaq-100 only includes the 100 largest non-financial stocks in the Nasdaq Composite Index (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC). It excludes financial stocks, which account for about 3% of the index, because they're more dependent on interest rate cycles than on innovation and organic growth. The Nasdaq-100 is rebalanced quarterly and reconstituted annually, so it also gives investors steady exposure to the top-performing stocks.

VOO and QQQ hold many of the same stocks, but QQQ uses a modified market-cap weighting system to prevent the largest companies from dominating the index. That's why Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) -- the top holding for both indexes -- accounts for 8.39% of VOO but only 8.10% of QQQ. But VOO usually holds smaller slices of other top stocks -- including Apple and Microsoft -- because it's more broadly diversified.

Which ETF is a better long-term buy?

Both of these ETFs are reliable investments for investors who don't have the time to micromanage individual stocks. But if I had to choose one over the other, I'd pick QQQ because it holds all of the winners without any exposure to the S&P 500's slower-growth stocks. QQQ's focus on growth might make it more volatile than VOO during market downturns, but it's designed to deliver bigger long-term gains for investors who can tune out the near-term noise.

title: If the Stock Market Crashes, This Is the First ETF I'm Loading Up On
detail:
If the Stock Market Crashes, This Is the First ETF I'm Loading Up On
Justin Pope, The Motley Fool

NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stock market will crash again at some point. There have already been numerous boom-and-bust cycles throughout the stock market's history, making the next crash more a matter of when than if.

Unfortunately, nobody actually knows when it will happen. Therefore, the best way to defend against a stock market crash is to have a plan for when the time comes. When it does, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ) could be the first exchange-traded fund (ETF) I load up on.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The QQQ holds the best AI stocks money can buy

Artificial intelligence (AI) has driven the stock market higher for several years now. It's not a fluke; AI has become arguably the most important technology in decades.

Image source: Getty Images.

The Invesco QQQ offers remarkably broad exposure to most companies involved in the AI trade. The ETF tracks the Nasdaq-100, an index filled with the world's most prominent technology companies.

Of course, that means a heavy lean into AI. Investors will find Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Micron Technology, Meta Platforms, Alphabet, and Tesla among the ETF's top holdings. That covers GPUs and memory for data centers, the hyperscalers, and even emerging industries, such as autonomous driving and robotics.

Why the next crash will probably create jaw-dropping buying opportunities

At the same time, excitement for AI has propelled the Nasdaq-100 and the Invesco QQQ. The ETF is up a whopping 98% over the past three years alone. Today, the stocks in the Nasdaq-100 trade at a blended price-to-earnings ratio of approximately 30. That's already a lofty valuation, and what if the AI boom slows and earnings deteriorate? That certainly wouldn't be good.

Tech stocks tend to outperform other sectors in bull markets. But that also means they tend to fall further during market downturns.

You can see how the QQQ has plunged during major market crashes, for instance, falling 83% following the burst of the dot-com market bubble in the early 2000s and about 50% during the financial crisis later that decade.

Data by

YCharts

I can't say with certainty that the AI craze will trigger a market crash. That said, there are risks.

The leading frontier model companies, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, are chasing massive market valuations while still logging hefty financial losses. It could become a big problem for the market if these AI companies continue to burn so much capital.

Key Points

Interested in SPDR Gold Shares? Here are five stocks we like better.

Monument Traders Alliance strategists suggest splitting portfolios between short-term volatility trades and longer-term, income-generating holdings amid current market turbulence.

Six simultaneous pressures, including Fed rate hikes, AI spending uncertainty and rising debt costs, have pushed the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.

Suggested plays include short-dated options on IWM, QQQ and GLD during 1% sell-offs, Agnico Eagle Mines for leveraged gold exposure, and Nuveen Municipal Value Fund for tax-free income.

Every portfolio in a volatile market has two jobs, and most investors only run one. Part of the money should be trading the noise. The rest should be getting paid to ignore it. The last few weeks have delivered 1% daily moves in both directions, and the reflex is to step back and wait for calm, but Bryan Bottarelli and Karim Rahemtulla of Monument Traders Alliance argue that waiting for a quiet tape is not a plan.

6 Pressures Hitting the Market at the Same Time

Count what the market is currently digesting. A midterm election cycle. A Federal Reserve that has returned to raising rates for the first time in more than three years, with the funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00% and futures pricing meaningful odds of another move before year-end. Inflation that consumers feel at the register. A federal debt load where interest expense now runs close to a fifth of annual tax receipts. Enormous AI-related capital expenditures (CapEx), with no settled view on whether those valuations are fair. And geopolitical conflict on top of it.

→ Bloom Energy Just Reported—Its Biggest Order Is Still Waiting on a Pipeline

Markets handle one or two of those at a time. Six is a different animal, which is why the 10-year Treasury yield touched levels not seen since 2002 earlier this month before easing back to near 5%.

That matters because the cost of money is now the story. AI buildouts that were funded with equity are moving to the bond market, and the bond market charges for risk in a way the stock market often does not.

→ Chefs' Warehouse Has Rallied 76%—Can the Stock Keep Climbing?

Why Forced Selling Creates the Better Entry Point

Rahemtulla frames fear as the mechanism, not the obstacle. The more volatile the tape, the more irrational the marginal seller, and the better the prices available to anyone who has already decided what they want to own. Bottarelli learned the same lesson on the trading floor: the moment everyone else stops out is the moment worth buying.
